headline: Concord man’s federal lawsuit adds to challenge of New Hampshire loitering law
dek: Robert Gaynor says the state statute gives police too much discretion to stop unhoused people; his case could be combined with an earlier lawsuit that survived a standing challenge.
body: A second unhoused man from Concord has filed a federal lawsuit challenging New Hampshire’s loitering-or-prowling statute, opening another legal front over how police may stop people in public spaces. Robert Gaynor, 42, filed the complaint Oct. 8 in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Hampshire, according to the [public case docket](https://dockets.justia.com/docket/new-hampshire/nhdce/1:2026cv00833/69049) and reporting by [New Hampshire Public Radio and the Concord Monitor](https://www.nhpr.org/nh-news/2026-10-12/loitering-law-newhampshire-lawsuit-aclu-concord).

Gaynor also asked the court to consolidate his case with a lawsuit filed in September 2025 by Robert Clark, another man who was unhoused in Concord when the earlier case began. The docket identifies the case as Gaynor v. New Hampshire Attorney General and names John Formella as the defendant. The filing describes the dispute as a constitutional challenge to a state statute, not a criminal prosecution against Gaynor. A docket entry says the consolidation motion was filed Oct. 8 and lists Oct. 22 as a follow-up date for an objection; that scheduling entry is not a ruling on the merits.

The American Civil Liberties Union of New Hampshire represents both plaintiffs. In the new case, Gaynor’s complaint says he has been unhoused for seven years and currently sleeps outside in northern Concord. The complaint says he has faced loitering charges multiple times, including an encounter under the Water Street Bridge in which a judge later ruled that the seizure was unlawful. Those statements are allegations in a court filing, not findings that have been tested at trial. The state has not been found liable in the new case, and the public docket does not show a decision resolving the constitutional claims.

New Hampshire’s [RSA 644:6](https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/LXII/644/644-6.htm) makes loitering or prowling a violation when a person knowingly appears at a place or time under circumstances that warrant alarm for the safety of people or property nearby. The statute lists factors that may contribute to that alarm, including fleeing when an officer appears, concealing oneself or an object, possessing tools that could suggest a crime is about to occur, or examining entrances to a building without a legitimate purpose. Before an arrest, the law generally requires an officer to give the person an opportunity to identify themselves and explain their presence, unless flight or other circumstances make that impossible.

Gaynor and Clark argue that the law is too vague and violates the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments. Their position, as summarized by NHPR and the ACLU, is that the statute allows stops and searches to turn on an officer’s subjective judgment about whether conduct looks alarming. The state statute itself does not mention homelessness. The plaintiffs’ argument is about how the law is written and enforced, including whether broad discretion makes ordinary conduct such as standing, walking or resting vulnerable to police intervention.

The new case builds on a dispute that has already produced a significant procedural ruling. The ACLU says a federal judge denied the state’s motion to dismiss the earlier Clark lawsuit on standing grounds on Aug. 28. Clark has since found housing and lives in Franklin, but he continues to return to Concord for services and to visit his father, according to NHPR. Gaynor’s consolidation request could allow the court to consider the two cases together, although the judge must still decide whether consolidation is appropriate and how the cases should proceed.

The filings also put local enforcement data into the debate. ACLU data cited by NHPR says Concord police brought 23 loitering cases in the 6th Circuit Court District Division between July 1, 2021, and June 30, 2023. Ten of those cases, or 43%, involved unhoused people, according to the organization. The ACLU separately counted about 260 loitering charges in 244 New Hampshire court cases during 2025, with more than 83% filed in the state’s circuit-court system. Those figures are the organization’s compilation of court data, not a state-issued finding that every charge was improper.

For Concord, the case focuses attention on the space between public safety and the treatment of people who have nowhere else to go. The law allows officers to investigate conduct that appears connected to a possible threat, while the plaintiffs say the same standard can turn ordinary presence in public into a police encounter. The legal question is therefore larger than Gaynor’s individual claims: a ruling could affect when officers may detain people, what explanations must be accepted, and how courts review similar cases across New Hampshire.

The immediate next step is procedural. The federal court must address Gaynor’s request to combine the cases, and the state will have an opportunity to respond to the complaint and consolidation motion. Until a judge rules, the allegations remain disputed and the statute remains in force. The public filings establish a new challenge and a request to join it to the earlier case; they do not establish that the law is unconstitutional or that every loitering charge involving an unhoused person was unlawful.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Concord man challenges New Hampshire loitering law in federal court
seoDescription: A federal lawsuit by Robert Gaynor adds to an ACLU-backed challenge of New Hampshire’s loitering statute and its use against unhoused people.
